sources.section: Store buffers, ordering and cache-line contention
sources.entry: x86-TSO: A Rigorous and Usable Programmer's Model for x86 Multiprocessors - The store-buffer model of Intel and AMD ordering, tested on hardware, fixing which reorderings a fence pays for.

summary.title: x86-TSO: A Rigorous and Usable Programmer's Model for x86 Multiprocessors
summary.one_liner: You learn why informal Intel and AMD x86 memory-ordering specs are ambiguous or unsound, and how the x86-TSO store-buffer abstract machine gives a precise, testable programmer's model.
takeaways: Store buffering lets two processors both read 0 in the SB test, so x86 is not sequentially consistent.
Early Intel and AMD x86 memory-ordering specifications were informal prose and contained ambiguities; some were unsound against real hardware (e.g. the n6 test).
x86-TSO models x86 as an abstract machine with FIFO store buffers per hardware thread, a global lock for LOCK'd instructions, and MFENCE flushing the buffer.
The model is formalised in HOL4 and proved equivalent to an axiomatic version, and it is used to reason about a Linux spinlock and data-race-freedom.
summary.summary: The paper reviews the Intel SDM and AMD64 manual memory-ordering specifications (pre-IWP, IWP/AMD3.14/x86-CC, Intel rev. 29-34, AMD3.15) using litmus tests such as SB, IRIW, n6, n5 and n4b, and shows that they are ambiguous, too weak, or unsound compared with real processors. It then presents x86-TSO, an operational abstract machine with per-thread FIFO store buffers, a global lock for LOCK'd instructions, and MFENCE flushing, with an equivalent axiomatic version; both are formalised in HOL4. The authors apply the model to correctness of a Linux spinlock and to a general theory of data-race-freedom for x86-TSO. The page is the CACM Research Highlights paper text.
